cues.text: Marshall's rule is clear, and it is wrong. Here are three facts that do not fit it. All three come straight out of the paper we are following.
hurdle rate. The return a firm insists a project must promise.
Here is what a firm's money costs it.
And here is what firms insist a project promises before they will build it. Three or four times as much.
Asked directly, firms named rates from eight to thirty per cent. The middle answer was fifteen. The average was seventeen.
And the safe cost of their money at the time? A nominal rate of four per cent, and a real rate close to zero.
Second. In the middle of the nineteen-eighties, American farmers stayed open through long stretches of losses.
In nineteen eighty-three the average net income for a farm operator was six thousand dollars. For the year.
Even leaving out the rent on the land and the mortgage payments altogether, it only rises to thirteen and a half thousand. For a whole family, for a year's work.
Marshall's rule says: stop. They did not stop.
exchange rate. How much of one country's money another's will buy.
imports. Goods made abroad and sold here.

Here is the dollar. Up sharply to the end of nineteen eighty-four — it rose by about fifty per cent — then falling from early nineteen eighty-five, until by the end of eighty-seven it was almost back where it had been in seventy-eight.
And here are the imports. Flat for three years while the dollar climbed. Then rising — and still rising, long after the reason for it had gone away.
The paper gives that level two different ways on two different pages. We use the first.
Firms turn down work that is profitable on paper.
Farmers absorb years of losses rather than shut.
And imports arrive years late, then refuse to leave.
They are not being stupid. The next four chapters explain why.
hurdle rates: 3–4× the cost of capital
farmers absorbed years of losses
imports arrived late — and stayed
